fields.foundation: The Byzantine Empire was not founded in any conventional sense. It was the surviving eastern half of the Roman Empire, a state that had dominated the Mediterranean world for centuries. Emperor Constantine I's dedication of Constantinople on 11 May 330 CE, on the site of the ancient Greek colony of Byzantion at the crossing of the Bosphorus, is the conventional founding moment of what later scholars called the Byzantine Empire, though its inhabitants called themselves Romans and recognised no break in Roman continuity. Constantine chose the site for its strategic strengths: it commanded the sea route between the Mediterranean and the Black Sea, gave access to Black Sea grain, and occupied a peninsula that any attacker had to assault by land and sea simultaneously. His gold coin, the solidus, introduced around 309 and struck at seventy-two to the Roman pound, about 4.5 grams of gold, was so reliable that it served as the Mediterranean world's leading international currency for some seven centuries. The eastern empire took on a lasting separate identity after the death of Theodosius I in 395 CE, when rule was divided between his sons Arcadius in the east and Honorius in the west, and the two halves were never again governed as one. The east proved more durable than the west: its urban culture was denser, its tax revenues greater, its frontiers more defensible relative to its resources, and it was better able to absorb, pay off or manage by diplomacy the pressure of barbarian peoples. The Theodosian Walls, whose main line was completed in 413 CE under Theodosius II and which were strengthened after an earthquake in 447 with an outer wall and moat, made the city effectively impregnable to any army that lacked both command of the surrounding waters and the means to breach the strongest fortifications of the age.
fields.socioeconomy: The Byzantine economy lasted eleven centuries. It rested on the stability of the gold solidus (later called the nomisma), on Constantinople's position at the crossroads of intercontinental trade, and on the agricultural surpluses of Anatolia and the Balkans. No earlier coin had served so long as a reliable international currency, and the solidus underpinned Byzantine commerce across the Mediterranean, the Black Sea and the routes to Persia and beyond: the sixth-century merchant Cosmas Indicopleustes claimed with pride that the emperor's coin was accepted from one end of the earth to the other. Constantinople stood at the junction of the Black Sea and Mediterranean trade systems, which allowed it to tax goods moving between the northern lands (grain, fish, furs and slaves) and the luxury markets of the south. The state also profited from tightly regulated industries such as silk, whose production it controlled after silkworm eggs were smuggled into the empire in the reign of Justinian. The heaviest economic blow was the Muslim conquest of the Levant and Egypt between 634 and 642 CE, which stripped away the empire's richest provinces and a large share of its tax revenue. The recovery under the Macedonian dynasty (867–1056) rested on a smaller but more coherent base: the Anatolian plateau supplied soldiers and grain, the revival of Balkan and Black Sea trade generated customs revenue, and the theme system of military landholding sustained frontier defence. In the chrysobull of 1082 Alexios I Komnenos granted Venice tax-free trade throughout the empire in return for naval support against the Normans. The grant gradually handed much of Constantinople's maritime commerce to Venetian merchants and created the dependency that later helped make the Fourth Crusade's diversion to Constantinople attractive to the Venetians.
fields.military: The Byzantine military system was among the longest-lived in history, and it changed a great deal over eleven centuries: from the late Roman field armies through the theme-based provincial defence system to the mercenary-heavy forces of the later empire. It kept enough capacity to preserve the state even through periods of catastrophic territorial loss. The empire's greatest military asset was Constantinople itself. Its walls withstood repeated sieges over eight centuries, by Avars and Persians in 626, Arabs in 674–678 and 717–718, Bulgarians and Rus', and each failure of an attacker bought the empire more time. In the second Arab siege of 717–718, Emperor Leo III used Greek fire to devastate the Umayyad fleet. Greek fire was an incendiary weapon whose exact composition remains unknown, reputedly introduced by the engineer Kallinikos around 672. It was the empire's most celebrated military secret; it burned even on water and was used to devastating effect against Arab and later Rus' fleets. The theme system, developed during the seventh and eighth centuries in response to the Arab conquests, reorganised the remaining empire into military-administrative districts whose soldiers were supported by land grants in return for service. The result was a largely self-sustaining provincial defence that reduced dependence on costly mercenaries. Basil II (r. 976–1025) used these resources to conquer Bulgaria after decades of war, earning the epithet Bulgar-slayer, and left the empire stretching from the Danube to northern Syria, its greatest extent since the seventh century. The decisive blow to Byzantine military power came at the Battle of Manzikert in 1071, where the Seljuk Turks under Alp Arslan defeated and captured Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes. The decade of civil war that followed allowed Turkmen groups to penetrate and permanently settle much of the Anatolian plateau, the heartland that had provided the empire's main source of soldiers and revenue for four centuries. The empire never recovered from this loss.
fields.governance: Byzantine government combined the Roman tradition of codified law and professional administration with a Christian ideology in which the emperor was God's chosen representative on earth and the patron and protector of the Orthodox Church. Justinian I's Corpus Juris Civilis consisted of the Codex Justinianus, Digest and Institutes, issued between 529 and 534 CE, and was later supplemented by his Novels (Novellae, new laws). It was the most systematic codification of Roman law ever undertaken. Italian legal scholars transmitted it to medieval and Renaissance Europe, where it became the foundation of the civil law tradition that shapes the legal systems of much of the world today. The Byzantine administration maintained a salaried civil service organised in elaborate hierarchies of titles, offices and precedence. It governed from the imperial palace through a network of themes and provincial centres, whose officials reported to Constantinople through chains of command kept working across great distances by the state post, the cursus publicus, known in Greek as the dromos. The relationship between emperor and church was close and in theory harmonious: the emperor summoned councils, influenced the choice of patriarchs and shaped religious policy, while the church legitimised imperial authority. In practice it was frequently contested, most dramatically during the Iconoclast controversy (c. 726–787 and 815–843 CE), when emperors who banned religious images were resisted by monks, clergy and popular piety in a conflict that severely damaged imperial authority. Diplomacy was arguably the empire's greatest achievement of government. Marriage alliances, trading privileges, subsidies, honorary titles and religious missions turned potential enemies into clients, neutralised threats and carried Byzantine culture far beyond the reach of its armies, as shown by the mission of Saints Cyril and Methodius to the Slavs of Moravia in 863 and the conversion of Bulgaria (864) and of Kievan Rus' (c. 988).
fields.impact: The Byzantine Empire influenced later history through four main channels: law, religion, language and the preservation of older culture. The Corpus Juris Civilis, rediscovered in late eleventh-century Italy and taught at Bologna and the universities that followed its model, became the foundation of European civil law and, through it, of the legal systems of most of the world outside the common law tradition. The Orthodox Christianity that the Byzantine state patronised and defined became the faith of Russia, Serbia, Bulgaria, Romania, Georgia and the Greek world, a “Byzantine commonwealth” that extended the empire's cultural reach far beyond its political frontiers. Byzantine libraries preserved the Greek language and the classical heritage of philosophy, literature and science. Scholars such as Manuel Chrysoloras carried it to Italy from 1397, as did émigrés after the empire's fall, and it helped shape the Italian Renaissance: the recovery of Plato and the Greek historians in Florence, Venice and Rome owed much to Byzantine scholarship. Constantinople was Europe's largest and richest city for much of the medieval period, with perhaps 400,000 to 500,000 people under Justinian, though only around 50,000 by the time of its fall. It was the commercial hub connecting the Black Sea, Mediterranean and overland trade systems, and a cultural capital whose art, architecture and literature set standards across the medieval Christian world. The Hagia Sophia, completed under Justinian in 537 CE, was the largest church in the world for nearly a thousand years. It is still standing, the supreme architectural achievement of late antiquity.
fields.decline: The Byzantine Empire declined over its final four centuries in full view of its own people. They could see the state shrinking but lacked the resources to stop it, and the period combined great cultural refinement with irreversible political contraction. The structural causes were set at the Battle of Manzikert in 1071, which opened the Anatolian plateau to permanent Turkish settlement and removed the demographic and agricultural base that had sustained Byzantine military power for four centuries. The Komnenian dynasty (1081–1185) recovered much ground through military reorganisation and diplomatic skill, exploiting the First Crusade to regain western Anatolia. The cost was trading privileges for Venetian merchants that drained Byzantine commercial wealth and created the incentive for the Fourth Crusade. In April 1204 the crusaders sacked Constantinople and established a Latin Empire that held the city until 1261. The capital that had withstood Persian, Arab, Bulgarian and Rus' sieges for eight centuries fell to fellow Christians, the Latins. Its treasures were looted, Hagia Sophia was desecrated, and its reputation for invincibility was permanently broken. The Palaiologan restoration of 1261, achieved by Michael VIII from the successor state of Nicaea, recovered Constantinople but not the empire's substance. Michael and his successors ruled a diminished state dependent on Genoese commercial privileges that reproduced the Venetian dependency in another form, and fourteenth-century civil wars hastened the decay. The final century and a half was one of steady Ottoman encirclement: the Ottomans established themselves in Europe at Gallipoli in 1354, moved their capital to Adrianople (Edirne), and reduced the empire to the city itself and scattered remnants in Greece. Constantine XI died fighting on the walls when Mehmed II took Constantinople on 29 May 1453. The last Roman emperor died in defence of the last Roman city, and eleven centuries of continuous institutional existence came to an end.
fields.summary: The Byzantine Empire survived for 1,123 years, one of the longest continuous imperial histories on record. It owed this to Constantinople's defences, the long stability of the gold solidus, the legal framework of the Corpus Juris Civilis and a diplomacy that repeatedly turned potential conquerors into clients and partners. It carried Roman civilisation into the medieval world and preserved the Greek intellectual heritage that would help start the European Renaissance.
fields.teaser: The Eastern Roman Empire survived nearly a thousand years after the fall of Rome in the West, preserving classical knowledge and Orthodox Christianity. Constantinople fell to the Ottomans only in 1453.
fields.t0: The eastern Roman Empire, ruled from Constantinople, whose people called themselves Romans for over 1,100 years.
fields.t1: It preserved Roman law in Justinian's Code and Greek learning, and spread Orthodox Christianity to Russia and the Balkans.
fields.t2: Manzikert in 1071 and the crusader sack of 1204 crippled it; the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453.
fields.dyk: Hagia Sophia, completed under Justinian in 537, remained the largest church in the world for nearly a thousand years.
